title: Satisfactory safety and immunogenicity of MSP3 malaria vaccine candidate in Tanzanian children aged 12-24 months.
ehr_evidence: Participant information was captured on paper case report forms (CRFs), which were double-entered into a Microsoft Access data base.
summary: A double-blind, randomized, dose-escalation Phase Ib trial assessed the safety and immunogenicity of the MSP3 malaria vaccine candidate in 45 Tanzanian children aged 12-24 months in Korogwe.
key_findings: A total of 45 children were enrolled, 15 in each of the two MSP3 dose groups and 15 in the Engerix B group.
Grade 3 adverse events were infrequent; only five were detected throughout the study, all transient and resolved without sequelae, and no serious adverse event was related to MSP3.
The only major difference in reactogenicity was induration between MSP3 and Engerix B groups (Fisher's exact p-value = 0.07).
Both MSP3 dose regimens elicited strong cytophilic IgG responses (IgG1 and IgG3), with 100% and 86.7% of 15 μg responders showing an 8-fold increase at day 84.
Vaccination induced seroconversion in all vaccinees, with a mean titre ± SD of 10.68 ± 4.64 versus 6.12 ± 1.66 in European volunteers.
No significant difference was observed in haematology or biochemical parameters between vaccine groups.
captured_features: Solicited local adverse reactions (pain, swelling, induration, erythema, pruritus)
Solicited systemic reactions (fever, drowsiness, loss of appetite, irritability)
Anti-MSP3 antibody levels (total IgG, IgM, IgG1-IgG4 subclasses)
study_design: Double-blind, randomized, controlled, dose-escalation Phase Ib clinical trial
data_source_type: other (clinical trial with paper CRFs entered into a Microsoft Access database)
population: 45 healthy Tanzanian children aged 12-24 months in Kwashemshi village, Korogwe District, Tanzania
exposure_domain: vaccine (MSP3 malaria vaccine candidate adjuvanted with aluminium hydroxide)
limitations: Inherent design weakness for evaluating reactogenicity due to subcutaneous MSP3 administration versus intramuscular control vaccine.
Small sample size (45 children) limiting power to detect adverse events.
Low malaria transmission in the study area meant most children had little prior exposure, limiting generalizability to high-transmission settings.
